ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Indo Bangla Migrants Issue 
*661. SHRI K.B. KRISHANA MURTHY: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether India and Bangladesh have agreed to solve the migrants issue 
on the basis of their 1992 joint communique; 
(b) whether Dhaka has consistently and resolutely denied existence of its 
citizen on the Indian soil: 
(c) if so, whether India has presented detailed documentary proof in this 
regard; and 
(d) if so, Bangladesh Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE INTHE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS 
(SHRIVINODKHANNA):(a)to(d) AStatementisplacedontheTableoftheHouse. 
Statement 
(a) to (d) The Government has been concerned about large scale, illegal 
immigration from Bangladesh into India. The Government has been taking up 
the issue of illegal immigration with the Government of Bangladesh regularly. 
However, the Government of Bangladesh has been denying that large scale 
illegal immigration is taking place. 
2. During the visit of Mr. M. MorshedKhan, Foreign Minister of Bangladesh 
on February 13-15,2003, the issue of illegal immigration, including the need for 
tightening border control to prevent all kinds of illegal cross-border movement 
was discussed in detail. Further discussions were held during the Foreign 
Secretary level talks with Bangladesh on 29th April, 2003 and Director General-
level talks held between Border Security Force and Bangladesh Rifles on April 
27 to May 1,2003 in Dhaka. 
3. Following detailed discussions India and Bangladesh have committed to 
cooperate on the basis of the Joint Communique issued on 28th May, 1992 on 
1 

RAJYA S ABHA [8 May, 2003 ] 
the occasion of the visit of Her Excellency the Prime Minister of Bangladesh to 
India. Tighter border control is expected to lead to a decrease in the number of 
illegal migrants. 
4. Generally illegal immigrants do not possess travel or identity documents. 
However, when available evidence on illegal Bangladeshi nationals in India lias 
been shared, the Government of Bangladesh has taken back its nationals, after 
due verification of their nationality. 
SHRI K.B. KRISHNA MURTHY: Mr. Chairman, Sir, I would like to know fiom 
the hon. Minister whether the Government has taken a decision to repeal the 
IDMT Act, 1983. If so, has the Government all along felt that this was a major 
impediment in checking large-scale influx of migrants from the neighbouring 
countries? Part (b) of my question is: Has the Government of Assam expressed its 
apprehension that repealing of the Act would result in victimisation of minorities 
in the State? I would also like to know whether the Government is engaged in 
damage control of the situation arising out of the large-scale influx of migrants 
from Bangladesh. What are the reasons for not taking any preventive measures 
in the first place to check the entry of such illegal migrants into India? 
THE MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI YASHWANT SINHA): 
Sir, so far as the first part of the question is concerned, it is correct that the 
Cabinet has decided for the repeal of this Act. The repealing Bill will come to 
Parliament very soon and I am sure, the hon. Members would have an opportunity 
of discussing it. So far as part (b) of his question is concerned, I very humbly 
submit that it would not be right to say that the Government has not taken any 
steps. The Government has been taking steps all along to prevent illegal migration 
from Bangladesh and we have reasons to believe that in recent years we have 
met with considerable success also. 
SHRI KB. KRISHNA MURTHY: Is it true that various Government 
agencies are harassing bona fide minorities, i.e. Muslims of India, on the

harassed by the Government agencies while checking illegal migrants from

(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) Consequent to the grant of licenses for Cellular Mobile 
Telephone Sen ice (CMTS) to private op erators. Cellular Services were first 
started in the four Metro City Service Areas of Delhi, Mumbai. Kolkata and 
Chennai from August, 1995 onwards and thereafter in the Telecom Circle Service 
Areas beginning December. 1996. After adoption of New Telecom Policy-1999

(NTP-99) and shifting of the existing operators to the revenue sharing regime of 
NTP-99, additional licenses were granted to private operators: The cellular sen ice 
has been progressively rolled out by the private operators in the district 
headquarters and towns. According to information furnished by the Cellular 
Operators Association of India, about 1640 district headquarters and towns in 
various service areas across the countr y had been covered with the cellular 
service by March. 2003. Mahanagar Telephone Nigam Ltd. started its cellular 
sen ices from February, 2001 in Delhi and Mumbai. Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited 
(BSNL) also started providing the servi ces in most parts of the country from 
October. 2002 and have so far covered about 1020 cities and towns with the 
cellular sen ice by March, 2003. Private operators coupled with the Government 
operators are expected to cover more and more places with the Cellular Senice 
over a period of lime. 
The terms and conditions of the Licence for CMTS require that in the Metro 
City Sen ice Areas an operator has to cover 90% of the Sendee Area within one 
\ car. and in the Telecom Circle Senice Areas, 10% of the District Headquarters 
within ons year and 50% of the District  Headquarters within three years. The 
licensee is also permitted to cover any other town in a district iniieu of the 
District Headquarter. The choice of District Headquarters/towns to be covered 
and further expansion beyond 50% District Headquarters/towns shall lie with 
ihe licensee depending on his business decision. There is no mandatory 
requirement for coverage of 100% of the districts as well as coverage of rural 
areas. 
Expansion for fresh start of CMTS in J&K. Assam and North East Telecom 
Circles was not permitted earlier on considerations of security. Tins was however 
permitted with effect from 21st August, 2002. Accordingly? BSNL has plans to 
launch its cellular senices in Jammu and Kashmir in the near future. BSNL also 
has plans to launch its cellular senices in Assam and North East Telecom Circles 
during the current financial year.

*671.  SHRIMOOLCHANDMEENA:  
           DR. T. SUBBARAMIREDDY:

(a) whether U.S. has imposed sanctions on Pakistan; 
36

Ob) if so. whether U.S. got a report that Pakistan has indulged in proliferation 
of nuclear technology; 
(c) whether U.S. has provided proof to the Pakistan on these charges; 
(d) if so. whether this would have a greater implication on India's security; 
and 
(e) if so. Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS 
(SHRIDIGVIJ AY SINGH): (a) to (c) The United States announced on 31 March. 
2003 that it had imposed non-proliferation penalties on Pakistan's Khan Research 
Laboratory (KRL) on 24 March 2003. The United States also imposed non-
proliferation sanctions on the North Korea entity Changgwang Sinyong 
Corporation (CSC) on the same day. 
2. The U.S. State Department clarified on 01 April. 2003 that the United 
States made a determination to impose penalties on both CSC and KRL as a 
result of a specific missile-related transfer from CSC to KRL. It further clarified 
that these sanctions did not pertain to any other activity, including nuclear-
related ones, and that the U.S. Administration had carefully reviewed the facts 
relating to the possible transfer of nuclear technology from Pakistan to North 
Korea, and decided that the facts do not warrant the imposition of sanctions 
under applicable U.S.laws. 
3. Proliferation activities in India's ne ighbourhood have implications for 
India's security. Government's defence preparedness fully takes into account 
these developments. 
4. Imposition of these sanctions substantiates Government's assessment 
regarding clandestine proliferation links between Pakistan and North Korea. 
Government welcomes all efforts to a ddress proliferation concerns regarding 
Pakistan.

Council would not be in conformity with the UN Charter; 
(b") if so, in what manner the UN Charter deals with such a situation if it 
actually happens; and 
(c) Governments views in this regard and the diplomatic steps it visualises 
to avoid such a situation and for maintaining universal peace? 
Ti IE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS 
(SHRI DIGVIJ AY SINGH): (a) to (c) Speaking in the specific context of Iraq, 
which was an issue colore the Security Council on March 10, the UN Secretary 
General said "If the US and others were to go outside the Council and take 
military action it would not be in conformity with the Charter". 
The Charter envisages use of force in case of self-defence or as authorised 
by the Security Council under Chapter VII. 
The Government had expressed its sense of deep anguish at the resort to 
military action in Iraq, which in its view lacked justification and was avoidable. 
Government has been in contact with other Governments on a more effective 
role by the UN in avoiding such situations and in strengthening international 
peace and security.

Nuclear power generation capacity 
4958. SHRIPREM CHAND GUPTA: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased 
to state : 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have recently announced its intention 
to increase the nudearpower generation capacity from 2720 MW to 20,000 MW;

to the thermal power and the time-frame for its implementation? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE INTHE DEPARTMENT OF ATOMIC ENERGY 
(SHRI SATY ABRATA MOOKHERJEE): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The present nuclear power generating capacity in the country is 2720 
MWe. This is scheduled to grow to 6680 MWeby December, 2008 progressively 
by completion of eight nuclear power reactor units (2x540 MWe at Tarapur, 
Maharashtra, 2x220 MWe at Kaiga, Kamataka, 2x1000 MWe at Kudankulam,

construction. More projects, subject to the availability of funds, are planned so 
as to reach a total nuclear power capacity of about 10,000 MWe by end of XI 
Plan. The aim is to reach a total nucl ear power generating capacity of about 
20,000 MWe by the year 2020. 
The capital cost per MWe of nudearpower plants is about Rs. 5 crore/MWe 
at 2001 -02 prices. In regard to coal thermal power plants it is about 20% lower 
than that of nuclear. However, the cost of generation from nuclear power plants 
is comparable to that of contemporary thermal power plants at locations about 
800 to 1000 km. from the coal pit-heads.

opportunities for Free/Open Source Software (OSS), more specially GNU/Linux

Government Institutions, localisation, R&D, inclusion of these in the Curricula/

Technology (DIT) maintains a stance of strict technology neutrality, platform

Multi-level marketing and direct selling of goods 
5003. SHRI ANIL SHARMA: Will the Minister of CONSUMER AFFAIRS, 
FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether multi-level marketing, direct selling of goods and services is 
legal in India; 
(b) whether Government are aware that some multi-level marketing 
companies like JLI and Frontier Trading are unnecessarily being harassed by the 
authorities in different States including Delhi; 
(c) whether Government would take any preventive measures to ensure 
smooth functioning and to protect above companies against such harassment; 
(d) whether Government have received any representation from the above 
companies in this regard; and 
(e) if so, the action taken by Government thereon and by when all the 
States would be directed to stop such harassment? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI V. SREENIVASA 
PRASAD): (a) to (e) There is apparently no legal provision against marketing 
systems such as direct seli.ng/multi-level marketing of goods. However, some of 
these companies reportedly take deposits from agents in advance, complaints/ 
cases are lodged against them under the provisions of "Prize Chits and Money 
Circulation Scheme (Banning) Act, 1978". A few such cases are brought to our 
notice by some of these companies along  with their representation such as 
M/s. Frontier Trading, Mumbai, Cantos Marketing Private Ltd., Hyderabad etc. 
Legal provision in this regard has been examined. It was found that as long as 
these companies are selling goods in the normal manner just like any other form 
of marketing of goods. Government need not have to make any special measure 
for preventing the alleged harassment. The Government of India have written to 
the Governments of all States/Union Territories to distinguish between Companies 
dealing with activities coming strictly  under the purview of "Prize Chits and 
Money Circulation Scheme (Banning) Act, 1978 and those such as direct/ 
network/multi-level marketing dealing in the jurisdiction of goods so as to avoid 
harassment and commercial losses to bonafide investors.

Indo-Russian discussions on Iraq war 
5027. SHRI K. NATWAR SINGH : Will the Minister of EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state : 
(a) whether India and Russia had discussions regarding Iraq war and 
its impact on the situation in Afghanistan and the anti-terror campaign in the 
region. 
(b) if so. the points of discussions on these two important issues; 
(c) whether there is a similarity of approach between the two countries: 
and 
(d) if so, whether both the countries have agree to work together to 
impress the US to stop war against Iraq and start process of rebuilding of Iraq 
with full cooperation of Iraqi people? 
  THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS 
(SHRIDIGVIJAYSINGH):(a) Yes. 
(b) During the sixth meeting of the Indo-Russian Joint Working Group on 
Afghanistan held on 28 March,   2003 in Moscow, the two sides discussed. 
122 

[8 May, 2003] RAJYA S ABHA 
inter alia, the situation in Afghanistan and Iraq. The Minister of External Affairs and Mr. 
Igor lvanov, the Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Russian Federation, have also spoken 
to each other over telephone twice on 23 March and 24 April, 2003. The Iraq war was 
also discussed in these two telephonic conversations. The two sides shared their views 
about the military action against Iraq and expressed concern at the humanitarian 
situation in Iraq. India and Russia share the view that the military action against Iraq 
should not weaken the resolve of the international community to fight terrorism in 
Afghanistan and in the region. Discussions on Afghanistan included the progress in 
implementation of Bonn Agreement of December 2001, and coordination of various 
international efforts aimed at rehabilitation and reconstruction. India and Russia also 
discussed the threats to regional peace and stability from terrorist activity in the region, 
and efforts aimed at strengthening international mechanisms to fight against 
international terrorism. They expressed serious concern over the escalation of 
subversive and terrorist activity by the Taliban and Al Qaida remnants and others 
in Afghanistan and their efforts to regroup with support from the outside. 
(c) Yes. 
(d) India's position on these issues is reflected in the Resolution adopted by the 
Parliament of Indie on 8 and 9 April, 2003. 
Withdrawal of sanctions against civilian technology by U.S.A. 
5028. DR.T.SUBBARAMIREDDY: SHRIK. NATWAR 
SINGH: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether American sanctions against India on civilian technology have 
been lifted; 
(b) if so, whether this was possible by follow-up paperwork done by the 
Political Advisor to the Prime Minister during his visit to Washington in the month 
of December, 2002; 
(c) if so, to what extent U.S. Government has finally cleared the US 
technology transfer to India; and 
(d) to what extent it would be helpful to India? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI 
DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) In September 2001, the United States had lifted all sanctions 
against India imposed after the nuclear tests in May 1998. including 
123 

RAJYA SABHA [8 May, 2003] 
on export of dual use' technologies to India. However, the United States 
continues to maintain some restrictions on such exports on the basis of its 
domestic law and its obligations to the international non-proliferation regimes. 
(b) The subject of broader access for India to U.S. controlled 'dual use' 
goods and technologies has beeen an im portant element of bilateral dialogue 
with the United States at all levels, including during the National Security 
Adusor's visit to Washington D.C. in December 2002.

5030. SHRI K.B. KRISHNA MURTHY: Will the Minister of EXTERN AL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state :

have brightened with the Allies winning the war and the resultant change in the Iraqi 
regime;

and 
(c) whether India's ambivalent stand on the U.S. aggression on Iraq will come 
handy to leverage the recovery of Iraqi dues?

VINOD KHANNA) : (a) to (c) The Government of India and the Government of Iraq

placed on progressive institutionalization for providing timely and adequate credit

society to enable them to adopt modem technology and improve practices for increasing 
agriculture production and productivity. An amount of Rs. 7,36,570 crore is estimated as

through Rural Employment Generation Programme (REGP). The scheme envisages that

money". For projects above Rs. 10 lakhs and upto Rs. 25 lakhs, rate of margin money

Removal of quantitative restrictions 
5096. SHRISURESH PACHOURI : Will the Minister of SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have made any assessment regarding the role of Small 
Scale Industries reservations in the backdrop of the removal of quantitative restrictions; 
(b) if so, details thereof; and 
(c) how Government propose to safeguard the interests of Small Scale 
Industries? 
THE MINISTER OF SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES (DR C.P. THAKUR): (a) and 
(b) The role of Small Scale Industries (SSIs) reservation in the backdrop of removal of 
Quantitative Restrictions (QRs) is constantly being assessed/ monitored by the 
Government. While the removal of QRs on imports has implied greater integration of the 
Indian economy with the world, it is n ecessary that in the transition period 
employment, balanced regional growth and utilization of local resources by local 
entrepreneurs is promoted through support to SSIs. This is sought to be achieved 
through the policies and programmes for the Sector including the policy of reservation 
for exclusive manufacture in this sector. 
(c) To safeguard the interest of the Small Scale Industries, Government has 
already announced a Comprehensive Policy Package for SSIs on 30th August, 2000 in order 
to strengthen the SSI sector and enhance its competitiveness both 
172 

[8 May, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
domestically and globally. The package inter-alia provides for easier access to credit, 
availability of collateral free loans upto Rs. 25.00 lakhs, composite loans upto Rs. 25 
lakhs, capital subsidy for technology upgradation and improved infrastructure. 
SSI facing international competition 
5097 SHRI KRIPAL PARMAR : Will the Minister of SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Small Scale Industries are facing the international competition 
after the removal of quantitative restrictions under the World Trade Organisation 
arrangement from April, 2001; 
(b) if so, whether it is fact that the Small Scale Industries are facing a tough 
competition with China, Singapore and other countries whose product of better quality 
are available at cheaper prices in the Indian market; and 
(c) if so, steps being taken by Government keeping in view the above facts? 
THE MINISTER OF SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES (DR. C.P. THAKUR): (a) and 
(b) Removal of Quantitative Restrictions have exposed the SSIs to greater competition 
with China, Singapore and other countries. However, the Small Scale Industries in 
India have shown resilience to withstand the impact of phasing out quantitative 
restrictions as is evident from their track record. 
(c) Government is constantly monitoring the impact of the removal of 
Quantitative Restrictions (QRs) on the economy including the Small Scale Industries 
(SSIs) in the country. Even after the removal of QRs, protection to the industries is 
available in the form of raising custom duties upto the bound levels, imposing anti-
dumping duties and taking safeguard measures in case of surge in imports. Government 
has also put in place several measures to strengthen the small scale industries to make 
them globally competitive. These include special focus on areas such as technology 
upgradation, infrastructure assistance through cluster approach, timely availability of 
credit, adoption of modem management practices, use of electronic infrastructure and 
other IT applications to face the emerging challenges of trade liberalization.

THE CONSTITUTION (NINETY-FIFTH AMENDMENT) BILL, 2003 
AND 
THE CONSTITUTION (NINETY-SIXTH AMENDMENT) BILL. 2003 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE A ND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI 
JASWANT SINGH): Mr. Chairman, Sir, I move: 
* That the Bill further to amend the Constitution of India as 
passed by Lok Sabha be taken into consideration." 
This Constitution (Ninety-Fifth Amendment) Bill, 2003, seeks to 
provide for tax on services as a separate entry for taxation and for related 
Central legislation to govern various modalities in that respect. 
Sir, in most developed countries, goods and services are traded and 
taxed together. Taxation of services in India was started through the Union 
Budget, 1994-95, when it was levied, with effect from July 1, 1994, on 
stockbrokers, general insurance and tele phone services; if I am not mistaken, 
the hon. Leader of the Oppo sition was the author of th is initiative then. The 
power to levy tax on services is, howeve r, not specifically mentioned either in 
the Union List or the Stat e List in the Seventh Schedule of Constitution; Entry 
97 of the Union List, which gives power to the Centre for levy and collection of 
"any tax not mentioned in ei ther of List II and List III". At present, therefore, 
Parliament has the power to levy and collect tax on services only as a residual 
taxation matter. In exer cise of this power, the Central Government has 
periodically taxed selected services. 
Sir, the role of this sector in t he economy being significant - with the 
service sector accounting for 48-plus per cent of the GDP - and on the basis of 
deliberations between the State Gove rnments and the Central Government, 
also in accordance with the views of the recommendations of Expert 
Committees, it has been proposed to suitably amend the Constitution: (i) to 
introduce a new entry (Entry No. 92C- Taxes on services) in the Union List 
(List I) of the Seventh Schedule of the Co nstitution; (ii) to insert a new article 
268A in the Constitution to provide for levy of tax on services by the Union and 
collection and appropriation of the pr oceeds thereof by the Union and the 
States in accordance with principles to be laid down by a new law to be 
enacted by Parliament; (iii) after the proposed 
205 

RAJYA SABHA [8 May, 2003)  
amendments to the Constitution are effe cted, to enact a suitable Central 
legislation to provide for all necessary modalities, including levy of the tax on 
services by the Union Government and collection and appropriation of the 
proceeds of this tax, up to the prescribed ad valorem limits, by the Union and 
the States, respectively. 
After this proposed amendment to the Constitution is considered 
and passed by Parliament and ratified by the State Legislatures, suitable 
Central legislation will be enacted to provide for all necessary modalities, 
including collection and appropriation of the proceeds of taxes on services by 
the Union and the States, respectively. 
Sir, this proposed amendment will facilitate reforms in the Domestic 
Trade System and, most importantly, it will widen the tax base of the States, 
as and when this Bill, this taxation measure, begins to be effectively 
implemented. 
Sir, I must also add here that this is only an enabling provision that 
through the Constitution, we have the le vying and collecting of service tax by 
the Centre and the States. This woul d, significantly, increase the revenue 
receipt collection of the States. And,  it is only after this Constitution 
Amendment is adopted, we will be bringing forth a Bill as early as possible. We 
would have brought it in this Session itself, but for the delay that has taken 
place. And we will have a legislation on service tax proper, in which we will 
consider fully whether the tax is to be shared or the services are to be shared, 
and it will be entirely possible because it is not practical for the Centre to tax all 
the services; and there are some services for which it will be more practical to 
leave them entirely in the care of the States. Now, these are the details, which 
will be taken up when this Bill proper for services tax comes up. This is only an 
enabling provision. I thought I should emphasise this. 
The question was proposed. 
DR. MANMOHAN SINGH (Assam): Sir, I rise to support this Bill. The 
fiscal system of our country is under great strain. In fact, the fiscal deficit of the 
Centre and the States, which now exce eds nearly 11 per cent of our Gross 
Domestic Product, is among the highest in the developing countries. Efforts 
have been made from time to time to tackle the fiscal malaise particularly the 
control of expenditure. Promises have been made, but, unfortunately, in 
particular, with regard to expenditure co ntrol, the last five years have seen 
retrogression, not progression.  In the same way, in the 
206 

[8 May, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
last decade, a good deal of attenti on has been paid to reforming the tax 
system of our country. But the sad rea lity is that the tax:GDP ratio in our 
country today is 2:2.5 per cent of the GDP lower than what it was some 10-12 
years ago. Therefore, we have to pond er over the conseq uences of the way 
the fiscal system of India is being ma naged. Emphasis has to be laid both on 
expenditure control and tax reform, with a tighter tax administration. These are 
the obvious routes to bring the fiscal system of our country into a proper 
shape. 
It was in this context that when I was the Finance Minister, we began 
the practice of taxing the services that the hon. Minister haa mentioned. It was 
in the Budget of 1994-95 that, for the first time, services were brought within 
the purview of the Union taxation. There is no explicit En try in Schedule VII, 
either in the Union List or  in the State List, which mentions the taxation of 
services. Therefore, at that time, we took advantage of Entry 97 of the Union 
List, which enables the Union Govern ment to tax items, which are not 
mentioned otherwise in either the Unio n List or the State List. This is, 
obviously, not a very satisfactory arran gement and, therefor e, the decision of 
the Government to get the Constitution amended to make an explicit provision 
for the taxation of services, and giving the Union the right to legislate about the 
basic principle on which this taxation should be based, is a sound one. 
[THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN in the Chair.] 
Also, the provision in the Constitutional amendment that the 
collection and appropriation will be the responsibility of both the Government 
of India and the States, in a manner to be prescribed by Parliament by law, I 
think, is also a sound provision. 
Madam, there are, however, two or three things that I would like to 
mention. India has premat urely graduated to the stat us of a service economy. 
In the history of the developing countries,  or, in the history of the developed 
countries, the stage when a country reaches  a position where 50 per cent of 
its GDP accounted for services, comes no rmally, much after industrialisation 
has progressed. Unfortunately, in our country, the pace of industrial growth 
has not been very rapid, and we have prematurely graduated to a service 
economy; the services today account for nearly 50 per cent of our GDP. The 
reasons for this are numerous. I do not wish to go into those reasons. But 
given the weight of services in our nation al economy,  it is entirely appropriate 
that services ought to be brought

to Parliament with a fresh legislation which will lay down the broad principles 
on which services ought to be taxed in our country. I would respectfully submit 
to him that adequate preparation should  be made for this purpose. The Bill, 
when it is ready, should be made available for discussion by the public. Those 
who are affected by the provisions of th is Bill, they should be consulted; and

that will add to the revenues of t he States. Having a service tax on the 
Concurrent List has certain difficulties, as I attempted to share my views with 
the hon. Member. For example, if we have the right to levy tax on the States, in

practical difficulties in this regard and that is why the entire arrangement of the 
Constitution has been structured, as the eminent jurist, Mr. Nariman, pointed 
out, in a particular manner. For example, this right were available with the 
States - and, say, it is the right of insu rance - State "A" might levy 10 per cent

non-existent and some States  might benefit by the exis tence of a wide variety

therefore, mandatory and th e duty of the Union Government to arrive at as 
uniformed structure of taxation as possi ble. Therefore, when introducing the

some unforeseen reason, the 2001 Census is delayed; the figures are 
delayed, would we run into a situati on where we are caught between two 
stools, as the phrase is used, so that we have no figures available as to how 
the next set of elections are to be conducted? That, I am afraid, may not be 
necessary because under the Constitution itself, they had visualised the 
situation of this kind happening, and both in article 82 relating to the 
composition of the seats for the House of  People, that is, the Lok Sabha, and 
in article 170 for the composition of s eats of the Legislative Assemblies, the 
second proviso to article 170 (3), and the second proviso to article 82 (3) itself 
clarifies this. I will just read out the proviso: "Provided further that such 
readjustment shall take effect from such  date on which the President may, by 
order, specify. And until such readjustment takes effect, any election to the 
Legislative Assembly may be held on bas is of the territorial constituencies 
existing before such readjustment.* In fact, whenever we read this Constitution 
document, we appreciate those who drafted this document because almost 
every conceivable contingency has been taken care of at the time of the 
drafting of the original text. So, the orig inal Constitution was so drafted that a 
contingency of this kind, where the ne xt figures are not available, we don't 
jump into a situation of vacuum where we  have no figures available. That is a 
situation where article 170 and article 82 have a proviso which deals with the 
situation. Therefore, I do  hope that such a situation may not arise. Madam, 
with regard to the number of consti tuencies, the hon. Member, and my 
colleague had raised this question, and some Members had also raised this 
question about reservation of constituencies for the Scheduled Castes and the 
Scheduled Tribes voters and electorates.  A conscious decision has already 
been taken

figure; in proportion to that figure, the reservation of constituencies would take 
place. With these words, I commend to this House that this amendment to the
